**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0760), Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections. All the questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sections: SECTION A (1800 - 1922), questions 1 to 4; SECTION B (1922 - 1961), questions 5 to 8; SECTION C (1961 to present), questions 9 to 12.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire historiographique, sans accès à un manuel pendant la rédaction ; aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée. Les dates et les faits cités sont ceux de l'historiographie courante du Cameroun, mais n'ont pas pu être recoupés avec une source écrite : à relire par un historien avant publication.

Q4 : dates et noms de mémoire, sans recoupement : défaite britannique à Garua (fin août 1914) et à Nsanakong (septembre 1914), prise de Douala le 27 septembre 1914, chute de Yaoundé le 1er janvier 1916, reddition de Mora en février 1916, internement des survivants au Rio Muni ; noms des commandants alliés (Dobell, Aymerich) ; exécution de Rudolf Douala Manga Bell en août 1914. questions.enonce_markdown:
Account for the early successes and subsequent defeat of Germany in Cameroon during the First World War.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** When the First World War began in August 1914, Germany held Kamerun, which was surrounded by British Nigeria, French Equatorial Africa and the Belgian Congo, while the Spanish colony of Rio Muni lay to the south. The Allies decided to conquer Kamerun. In the first weeks the German forces won several battles, but they were beaten in the end: Douala fell in 1914, the capital Yaounde in January 1916, and the last German forces left in February 1916. This essay explains both the early successes and the final defeat.

**1. Reasons for the early German successes (1914)**

- **Good defensive preparation and knowledge of the terrain.** The German colonial force (the Schutztruppe) and the police, made up of Germans and African soldiers, were small but trained and disciplined, and they knew the rivers, forests and mountains. They fought from prepared positions and from forts, and used the railways to move troops quickly (interior lines).
- **Weak and uncoordinated Allied attacks at the start.** The first Allied operations were launched in haste and by separate columns from Nigeria, Chad and the Congo, which were not properly coordinated and often lacked good information. The British attack on the German fort at Garua in northern Cameroon (late August 1914) failed, and a British column was beaten at Nsanakong near the Nigerian border (September 1914).
- **Difficult conditions for the Allies.** The rainy season, the dense forest, the swamps, the lack of roads, tropical disease and supply problems slowed and weakened the Allied columns.
- **Surprise and the Allies' misjudgment.** The Allies had expected an easy campaign, and the Germans were not subdued quickly. The Germans also held strong positions in the north, such as Mora, which resisted for a long time.

**2. Reasons for the final German defeat**

- **Superior Allied numbers and resources.** The Allies had many more men and much more equipment, and they could bring reinforcements from Nigeria, the Gold Coast, French Africa and the Belgian Congo, whereas Germany received none.
- **Control of the sea.** The British navy blockaded the coast, so Germany could not send soldiers, weapons or medicines. The joint British and French force, with naval support, captured Douala on 27 September 1914. This was a decisive blow, since Douala was the main port and the railway terminus. The German administration, which had its seat at Buea, withdrew inland to Yaounde, and Buea fell in the following months.
- **Better Allied coordination.** After the early failures the Allies cooperated more closely under joint commanders (the British General Charles Dobell and the French General Joseph Aymerich), with simultaneous advances by British, French and Belgian troops from several directions. These columns slowly cut up the German territory and separated their forces.
- **German isolation and exhaustion of supplies.** Cut off from Europe and the sea, the Germans ran out of ammunition, food and medical supplies. Their forces were pushed back to the south and north, and were small compared with the Allies. The fall of Yaounde on 1 January 1916, after a long retreat, ended organised defence, and the garrison at Mora in the north, which had held out for a long time, surrendered in February 1916. Many Germans and their African soldiers escaped into Spanish Rio Muni, where they were interned.
- **Lack of support from the Cameroonian population.** German harsh rule (forced labour, taxes, punishment, and the execution of the Duala chief Rudolf Douala Manga Bell and others in August 1914) had created much resentment. Many Cameroonians therefore did not support the Germans, and some helped the Allies as guides, porters and soldiers.
- **The war in Europe.** Germany had to concentrate its efforts on the European front and could not strengthen a distant colony.

**Conclusion.** Germany's first successes were due to preparation, knowledge of the land and the poor coordination of Allied columns. Its defeat was due to the Allies' greater numbers, sea power, improved coordination, German isolation without supplies, and the lack of local support. By 1916 the Germans had left Cameroon, and the territory was later divided between Britain and France.
